terms.definition: A measure of how airtight your house is. Lower is better — it means less air leaking in and out through cracks. Tested with a blower-door test.
A designation that dramatically lowers your property taxes by assessing the land at its agricultural value instead of market value. You need to prove you're using the land for farming or ranching.
A home built using a metal post-frame building shell — like a big barn or shop — with a fully finished residential interior. Faster to build and cheaper than traditional stick-frame construction.
A type of insulation sprayed directly onto walls and roof. It expands to fill every gap, creating both insulation and an air barrier. The gold standard for barndominiums.
A large tank (usually 5,000-10,000 gallons) that stores rainwater or well water as a backup supply. Think of it as a giant water battery for your property.
A document NRCS creates WITH you that identifies what your land needs (clearing, fencing, water, etc.) and recommends specific practices. Required before EQIP can fund anything.
A government program where they pay a percentage of the cost for conservation work on your land. You do the work, they reimburse you. EQIP is the biggest one.
Your main point of contact at the local NRCS office. This person helps you develop your conservation plan and guides your EQIP application. Think of them as your government liaison.
In Oklahoma, you can drill a well and use water for your household, livestock, and up to 3 acres of irrigation without any permit. This covers everything a homestead needs.
The USDA's biggest cost-share program. They reimburse you 75-90% of the cost for conservation work on your land — things like clearing brush, building fences, and digging ponds.
A device that brings fresh air into your tightly sealed house while capturing the energy from the outgoing stale air. Keeps the air fresh without wasting heating or cooling.
A professional inspection that checks if the land has any contamination — old fuel tanks, chemical spills, industrial waste. Phase 1 is a records review. Phase 2 involves soil testing.
A unique number assigned to your property by the Farm Service Agency. It's free and takes about an hour to get. You need this before you can apply for ANY USDA program including EQIP.
A map showing which areas are at risk of flooding. If your building site is in a 100-year floodplain, insurance costs go up dramatically and building gets complicated. Always check before buying.
A heavy machine that grinds trees, brush, and stumps into mulch right where they stand. Turns overgrown land into cleared ground in hours instead of days.
The USDA office that handles farm numbers, crop reporting, and some loan programs. Usually in the same building as NRCS. Your first stop after buying land.
A Texas-specific local authority that may regulate how much water you can pump from your well. Oklahoma doesn't have these — it's one reason OK is simpler for well water.
How fast your well can produce water. A household needs at least 5 GPM for comfortable living. Less than 3 GPM means you'll need a storage tank to buffer demand.
A score that measures how energy-efficient your home is. Lower is better. A typical new home scores around 100. Our target is much lower than that.
A water heater that uses a heat pump instead of electric coils or gas burners. Uses about 1/3 the electricity of a standard electric water heater.
A 275-gallon plastic tote in a metal cage. Commonly used as fish tanks in aquaponics systems because they're cheap, food-safe, and widely available.
A dog breed (like Great Pyrenees or Anatolian Shepherd) that lives with your livestock and protects them from predators. Not a pet — a working animal.
The three main systems inside a building: HVAC (mechanical), wiring (electrical), and water/drain pipes (plumbing). These all get 'roughed in' before insulation and drywall.

The legal right to extract oil, gas, and minerals from under the land. In Oklahoma and Texas, these are often separated ('severed') from the surface rights. The person who owns the minerals can legally access the surface to drill — even if you own the land above.
An all-in-one heating and cooling system. A small unit on the wall connects to an outdoor compressor. No ductwork needed. Very efficient and perfect for barndominiums.
The USDA agency that runs EQIP and other conservation programs. They help landowners improve their land with cost-share funding. Your district conservationist works here.
The state agency that regulates oil and gas activity in Oklahoma. Search their records to check if there are any active wells or leases on land you're considering buying.
The state agency that manages water rights and well records in Oklahoma. You can search their database for well logs near any property.
A soil test that measures how fast water drains through the ground. Required before installing a septic system — the results determine what type of system your property needs.
Flexible plastic tubing used for water supply lines. Much easier to install than copper — you can bend it around corners without fittings. The go-to for DIY plumbing.

A building method where large posts set in the ground (or on piers) support the roof. No traditional foundation needed. This is how barns, shops, and barndominiums are built — faster and cheaper than stick-frame.
A numbered code for a specific type of conservation work. Code 314 is brush management, 382 is fencing, 378 is ponds. Each code has its own payment rates and standards.
The window when NRCS scores and ranks all EQIP applications. The national deadline is January 15, but states have additional periods. Your application competes against others in your area.
An on-site wastewater treatment system for properties without city sewer. In rural Oklahoma and Texas, an aerobic septic system is usually required. Must be installed by a licensed contractor.
When the mineral rights have been separated from the surface rights in a property's deed history. Very common in Oklahoma and Texas. Means someone else might own what's under your land.
A loan that combines land purchase + construction + permanent mortgage into one closing. You lock your interest rate upfront and only go through the paperwork once.
A free USDA database that shows the soil types on any property. Helps you understand what will grow well, whether septic will work, and how the land drains.
When a consulting forester walks your property and inventories every tree — species, size, quality, market value. This is how you find out what the trees on your land are worth.
A document from a title company showing who owns the property, any liens or debts attached to it, and the terms under which they'll insure your ownership. Never buy land without this.
The federal department that oversees farming, food, and rural development. FSA, NRCS, and Rural Development are all under the USDA umbrella.
A sheet material (like Tyvek) wrapped around the outside of a building to block wind and rain while still letting moisture vapor escape. Part of the building envelope.
